title: Bài sưu tầm 213 - Passage 2: Tapping the Earth's Cauldron: The Geothermal Frontier
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 213

Tapping the Earth's Cauldron: The Geothermal Frontier

Paragraph 1. Deep beneath the volcanic basalt plains of Iceland lies an energy reserve of staggering proportions. While most countries depend on burning hydrocarbon fuels or harnessing variable surface phenomena like wind and sunlight, Iceland derives nearly one hundred percent of its electrical generation and building heat from domestic renewable sources, primarily geothermal energy. Straddling the Mid-Atlantic Ridge—a tectonic boundary where the North American and Eurasian plates slowly tear apart—Iceland is a geological hotspot where subterranean magma ascends unusually close to the Earth's crust. For over a century, engineers have exploited this subterranean cauldron, transforming an impoverished island once dependent on imported coal and peat into a global beacon of clean energy independence.

Paragraph 2. The technical foundation of conventional geothermal power relies on hydrothermal circulation. In natural geothermal fields, rainwater percolates through porous volcanic fractures deep into the crust, where it comes into direct proximity with magma chambers heated to several hundred degrees Celsius. Subjected to intense subterranean pressure, the water superheats without boiling. When engineers drill production boreholes down into these high-enthalpy reservoirs—typically between one and three kilometres below the surface—the sudden drop in pressure causes the superheated fluid to flash violently into high-pressure steam. This steam is funnelled upward through steel pipes to spin massive electromagnetic turbines, generating baseload electricity before being condensed back into liquid water.

Paragraph 3. In the capital city of Reykjavik, geothermal energy's most transformative civic application is district heating. In the early twentieth century, the city was shrouded in choking smoke produced by burning soft coal to warm drafty timber homes. Beginning in 1930, municipal authorities constructed an insulated underground pipeline network carrying geothermal water from nearby boreholes directly into urban radiators. Today, this municipal system heats over ninety-nine percent of homes in the greater Reykjavik area at a fraction of the cost of fossil fuels. The municipal thermal grid is so abundant that excess thermal runoff is pumped through coiled plastic conduits embedded directly beneath city pavements and sidewalks, melting winter snow and ice automatically without the need for toxic chemical de-icing salts or snowploughs.

Paragraph 4. Despite its triumphant record, geothermal extraction is not devoid of environmental complications and operational hazards. Magma-heated reservoir fluids are rarely pure water; they contain significant concentrations of non-condensable dissolved gases, primarily carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide. If vented directly into the ambient atmosphere, hydrogen sulfide produces a noxious rotten-egg odor and can trigger respiratory inflammation in downwind communities. To neutralize this emissions hazard, engineers at the Hellisheidi geothermal plant developed the Carbfix project. Non-condensable gases are captured at the turbine exhaust, dissolved under pressure into massive streams of wastewater, and reinjected deep into porous basalt formations. Within two years, chemical reactions between the acidic fluid and basalt minerals permanently transform the dissolved gas into solid white carbonate stones, locking greenhouse gases underground forever.

Paragraph 5. Looking toward the future, geoscientists are pushing deep drilling technology to its absolute physical limits. Standard geothermal wells tap fluids at roughly three hundred degrees Celsius; however, the Iceland Deep Drilling Project (IDDP) is drilling boreholes nearly five kilometres deep to penetrate 'supercritical' reservoirs, where temperatures exceed four hundred and fifty degrees Celsius and pressures surpass two hundred atmospheres. Supercritical fluids exist in an exotic physical state that is neither liquid nor gas, carrying up to ten times more kinetic energy per volume than standard steam. A single supercritical borehole could produce as much electrical energy as ten conventional geothermal wells, dramatically shrinking the surface land footprint of future power plants. As nations seek dependable, weather-independent baseload power to replace coal, Iceland’s volcanic engineering proves that the molten core of the planet can power human civilization sustainably.

q14.text: Iceland relies on imported coal for the majority of its current electricity production.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...Iceland derives nearly one hundred percent of its electrical generation and building heat from domestic renewable sources..." → Mâu thuẫn trực tiếp với relies on imported coal.

q15.text: Superheated water flashes into steam when it experiences a sudden decrease in pressure.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...the sudden drop in pressure causes the superheated fluid to flash violently into high-pressure steam."

q16.text: Reykjavik's district heating network was first established during the early nineteenth century.

steps: Đoạn 3: "Beginning in 1930, municipal authorities constructed an insulated underground pipeline network..." → Năm 1930 là thế kỷ 20, không phải thế kỷ 19.

q17.text: Warm geothermal water is used to keep roads and walkways free of ice in Reykjavik.

steps: Đoạn 3: "...excess thermal runoff is pumped through coiled plastic conduits embedded directly beneath city pavements and sidewalks, melting winter snow and ice automatically..."

q18.text: The Carbfix project took more than ten years to convert its first batch of gas into stone.

steps: Đoạn 4: "Within two years, chemical reactions... transform the dissolved gas into solid white carbonate stones..." → Trong vòng 2 năm chứ không phải mất hơn 10 năm.
Đoạn 2: "...percolates through porous volcanic fractures deep into the crust..." (Distractors: chambers, reservoirs).
Đoạn 3: "...shrouded in choking smoke produced by burning soft coal to warm drafty timber homes." (Distractor: peat).
Đoạn 3: "...carrying geothermal water... directly into urban radiators." (Distractors: pipes, homes).
Đoạn 3: "...without the need for toxic chemical de-icing salts or snowploughs."
Đoạn 4: "...permanently transform the dissolved gas into solid white carbonate stones..." (Distractors: minerals, gases).
